To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the telomere shortness observed in children with cancer during chemotherapy is not permanent, and that telomere shorting is not useful to predict the risk of recurrence of childhood cancer.

1) children with standard-risk ALL do not suffer significant telomere shorting during therapy; 2) children with solid tumors suffer greater telomere shortning; and 3) serial telomerase determination is useful to follow-up ALL, but not solid tumors.
children with solid tumors have accelerated telomere shorting during treatment, whereas children with leukemia have little telomere loss.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of telomerases in the development and progression of childhood cancer.
the long-term impact of childhood cancer treatment on hematological cell telomeres and the role of telomerases as markers of pediatric cancer.
the study of telomere dynamics and telomerase expression during the course of pediatric cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

telomere shorting in children with solid tumors, but not in those with standard-risk ALL, is associated with the treatment, and that telomerase determination is a useful marker for disease remission in ALL, but not in solid tumors.
telomere length is a useful tool to assess disease activity and remission in childhood ALL, but not in childhood solid tumors.
, in children with solid tumors, chemotherapy-induced shortening of telomeres in hematopoietic stem cells may be a risk factor for the development of secondary leukemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children with ALL and solid tumor patients have different telomere shorting rates, and telomerase activity may have a role in monitoring disease remission in ALL, but not in solid tumors.
telomere dynamics in pediatric cancer is complex.
telomere length in hematopoietic stem cells and granulocytes is a reliable biomarker for the assessment of the long-term effects of cancer therapy on bone marrow and immune system function.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the long-term consequences on hematopoietics of pediatric cancer therapy, including the use of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, are still unclear, and that the use of telomere length measurements in MNC as a surrogate for hematopoietic senescence is not a useful clinical tool.
telomerase activity can be used to monitor the course of treatment in children with leukemia, while the role of telomerases in children with solid tumors is less clear.

the hematopoietic telomere length of children with ALL is not adversely affected by standard-risk therapy, but that of children with solid tumor is, with the degree of telomere shorting varying with the aggressiveness of the treatment.
